hello.title: Hello, Odin!
hello.summary: Write your first Odin program and print text and numbers with fmt.println and fmt.printf.
hello.lesson.0: Odin is a simple and fast programming language. This course uses Odin `dev-2026-11`, the release from November 2026. Every Odin program is made of **packages**. A program that you can run uses `package main` and has a procedure called `main`. Odin starts the program there.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `package main` says that this file belongs to the main package. `import "core:fmt"` loads the `fmt` package, which can print text. The prefix `core:` means that the package comes with Odin. `main :: proc()` defines the procedure `main`: `::` means "is defined as" and `proc` means procedure. Its code goes between the braces `{` and `}`.
hello.lesson.4: `fmt.println` prints its values, puts a space between them and ends the line. Text goes in double quotes and is called a **string**. Numbers have no quotes. `fmt.println()` without values prints an empty line.
hello.lesson.6: Odin can calculate for you. `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is only text. Use `*` to multiply and `/` to divide.
hello.lesson.9: `fmt.printf` prints a **format string** and fills in values. Each placeholder starts with `%`: `%s` for a string, `%d` for a whole number and `%v` for any value. `printf` does not end the line, so you add `\n` (a new line) yourself. `fmt.printfln` works the same way but ends the line for you.
hello.lesson.11: A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and Odin ignores it. You do not need a semicolon `;` at the end of a line.
hello.lesson.12: Odin is case sensitive: `fmt.println` works, `fmt.Println` does not exist. Text needs double quotes: `"Hi"` is a string, `'Hi'` is an error.
hello.card.0: `package main` + `main :: proc()` make a runnable program
hello.card.2: `fmt.println(a, b)` prints with spaces and a new line
hello.card.3: `fmt.printf("%s %d %v\n", s, n, x)` fills in values
hello-1.prompt: Which procedure does Odin run when the program starts?
hello-1.explain: A runnable program starts in the procedure `main` of the package `main`.
hello-2.explain: `println` puts a space between its values.
hello-3.explain: `10 - 4` has no quotes, so Odin calculates `6`. Then `println` adds a space and the text.
hello-4.explain: `printf` prints exactly the format string. You need `\n` at the end to start a new line, or you use `printfln`.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Hi.
hello-5.explain: The package name goes in double quotes, with the prefix `core:` for packages that come with Odin: `import "core:fmt"`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Name: Ada`.
hello-6.explain: `%s` is the placeholder for a string. `%d` only works for whole numbers.
hello-7.prompt: Build the line that prints Hello, Odin! on its own line.
hello-7.explain: The procedure is `fmt.println` in lower case. The text goes in double quotes inside the parentheses.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a complete program.
hello-8.explain: First the package, then the imports, then the procedure `main` with its code between the braces.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.

hello-11.explain: Odin is case sensitive. The procedure is `fmt.println` in lower case.

variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, get to know int, f64, string and bool, and fix values with constants.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** stores a value under a name. `name := value` creates a new variable: `:=` declares it and gives it its first value. Later, `=` changes the value of a variable that already exists.
variables.lesson.3: Every variable has a **type**, and it never changes. `int` holds whole numbers, `f64` decimal numbers, `string` text and `bool` the values `true` or `false`. With `:=` Odin picks the type from the value. You can also write it yourself: `name: type = value`. A variable without a value starts with its **zero value**: `0` for numbers and `false` for `bool`.
variables.lesson.6: Odin knows `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and `%` gives the remainder of a division. When you divide two `int` values, Odin drops the remainder: `7 / 2` is `3`. With decimal numbers, `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`. `x += 5` is short for `x = x + 5`; `-=`, `*=` and `/=` work the same way.
variables.lesson.8: Odin never mixes types on its own: an `int` plus an `f64` is an error. You convert a value with the name of the type, like a procedure call: `f64(n)` makes a decimal number, `int(x)` makes a whole number and drops the decimals.
variables.lesson.11: `::` declares a **constant**: a value that is fixed when the program is compiled. You cannot change a constant later. You already know `::` from `main :: proc()`: the procedure `main` is a constant too.
variables.lesson.13: `:=` creates a new variable, `=` changes an existing one. Using `:=` twice for the same name in the same block is an error. Odin has no `x++`: write `x += 1`.
variables-2.explain: `f64` holds decimal numbers. An `int` holds only whole numbers.
variables-3.explain: The second line uses `:=` again, so it declares `x` a second time. To change the value, write `x = 6`.
variables-4.explain: Both numbers are `int`, so `17 / 5` drops the remainder and gives `3`. The remainder `%` is `2`.
variables-5.explain: Variables without a value get their zero value: `0` for `int` and `false` for `bool`.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 15.
variables-6.explain: `total += 5` adds 5 to `total`. `=+ 5` would set it to `+5`, and `:=` would declare it again.
variables-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.5.
variables-7.explain: `f64(n)` converts `n` to a decimal number, so the division keeps the `.5`. With `int` the result would be `3`.
variables-8.prompt: Build the line that declares the variable `price` with the type `f64` and the value `2.5`.
variables-8.explain: First the name, then `:` and the type, then `=` and the value.
variables-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 50.
variables-9.explain: `count` starts at 3, becomes 5 and then 50. Only then is it printed.
variables-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
variables-11.explain: `price` is an `f64` and `count` is an `int`. Convert first: `total := price * f64(count)`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program decide with if, else and switch, and combine conditions with &&, || and !.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition needs no parentheses, but the code always goes between braces `{` and `}`.
conditions.lesson.2: A comparison gives a `bool`. `==` means equal, `!=` not equal, and there are `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Note the difference: `=` changes a variable, `==` compares two values.
conditions.lesson.4: `else` runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if` you test more conditions one after the other. Odin runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.
conditions.lesson.6: You can combine conditions: `&&` means and (both must be `true`), `||` means or (at least one must be `true`), and `!` turns `true` into `false` and the other way round.
conditions.lesson.9: `switch` compares one value with several cases. A `case` can list several values, separated by commas. `case:` without a value is the default: it runs when no other case matches. Odin runs only the matching case and never continues into the next one, so you need no `break`.
conditions.lesson.11: A `switch` without a value works like a chain of `if` and `else if`: every case is a condition, and the first `true` one runs.
conditions.lesson.13: The condition must be a `bool`. `if 1 { }` is an error, and so is `if x = 5 { }`: write `if x == 5 { }`.
conditions-1.explain: `7 > 5` is `true`, so the first block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `85 >= 90` is `false`, but `85 >= 80` is `true`, so Odin prints `B` and skips the rest.
conditions-3.prompt: Which operator checks if two values are equal?
conditions-3.explain: `==` compares two values. `=` changes a variable, `:=` creates one and `!=` means not equal.
conditions-4.statement: In a `switch`, Odin continues with the next case after the matching one unless you write `break`.
conditions-4.explain: Odin runs only the matching case. There is no fall through, so you need no `break`.
conditions-5.explain: `||` needs only one `true` side. `b > 5` is `true`, so the whole condition is `true`.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints adult.
conditions-6.explain: `>=` means greater than or equal, so `18 >= 18` is `true`. `18 > 18` is `false`.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints both only when `a` and `b` are both positive.
conditions-7.explain: `&&` is `true` only when both sides are `true`. Here `b > 0` is `false`, so the program prints `not both`.
conditions-8.prompt: Build the first line of an `if` that checks whether `x` is greater than 10.
conditions-8.explain: `if`, then the condition, then the opening brace. Odin needs no `then`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order: the code prints hot when `temp` is above 25 and not hot otherwise.
conditions-9.explain: The `if` block handles the `true` case, the `else` block all other cases.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
conditions-11.explain: Odin has no `default` keyword. The default case is written `case:`.
conditions-12.explain: `=` changes a variable. To compare, write `if x == 5 {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with the for loop: counting, ranges, loops with a condition, break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: Odin has only one loop keyword: `for`. The classic form has three parts, separated by semicolons: a start, a condition and a step.
loops.lesson.2: `i := 0` runs once at the start. Odin checks `i < 3` before every round and stops when it is `false`. `i += 1` runs after every round. Each run of the loop body is called an **iteration**.
loops.lesson.4: A **range** is shorter: `for i in 0..<3` counts `0`, `1`, `2`. The `..<` stops before the end. With `..=` the end is included, so `1..=3` counts `1`, `2`, `3`.
loops.lesson.6: A `for` with only a condition repeats as long as the condition is `true`. Other languages call this a while loop.
loops.lesson.8: A `for` without anything repeats forever. `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and starts the next one.
loops.lesson.10: A common pattern: a variable outside the loop collects a result, and every iteration adds to it.
loops.lesson.12: Odin has no `i++`, so the classic loop needs `i += 1`. The three parts have no parentheses around them.
loops-1.explain: `..=` includes the end, so the loop adds `2 + 3 + 4 = 9`.
loops-2.explain: `n` becomes 3, 9 and 27. Then `27 < 20` is `false` and the loop stops.
loops-3.prompt: How many times does this print Hi?
loops-3.explain: `0..=3` includes the end: `0`, `1`, `2` and `3` are four numbers.
loops-4.statement: `for i in 0..<5` also runs with `i` equal to `5`.
loops-4.explain: `..<` stops before the end. The loop runs with `0` to `4`.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints 0, 1 and 2.
loops-5.explain: The step `i += 1` adds one after every iteration. Odin has no `i++`.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints the numbers 1 to 5.
loops-6.explain: `..=` includes the end. With `..<` the loop would stop at 4.
loops-7.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts from 0 to 2.
loops-7.explain: `for`, the loop variable, `in` and the range. `0..<3` stops before 3.
loops-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 10.
loops-8.explain: Create `total` first, add every `i` inside the loop and print the result after the loop.
loops-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.

loops-11.prompt: This loop should print 1, 2, 4 and 5. Which line has the bug?
loops-11.explain: `break` ends the whole loop, so only 1 and 2 are printed. Use `continue` to skip only 3.
loops-12.explain: `i` becomes 7, 4, 1 and then -2. Only then is `i > 0` `false`.
procedures.title: Procedures
procedures.summary: Write your own procedures with parameters and return values, including procedures that return several values.
procedures.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a named block of code that you can run (call) as often as you like. You declare it like `main`: a name, `::` and `proc`. To call it, write its name and parentheses.
procedures.lesson.2: **Parameters** are the inputs of a procedure. Each one has a name and a type, like `name: string`. Several parameters with the same type can share it: `a, b: int`. The values you pass when you call the procedure are called **arguments**.
procedures.lesson.5: `-> int` after the parameters says that the procedure gives back an `int`. `return` ends the procedure and gives the value back to the caller. You can store the result in a variable or use it directly.
procedures.lesson.7: A procedure can return several values. Put the types in parentheses, `-> (int, int)`, and separate the values with commas after `return`. The caller receives them with several names: `q, r := divide(17, 5)`.
procedures.lesson.9: Odin code often returns a `bool` as the last value to say if everything worked. The caller can then check `ok`.
procedures.lesson.11: The order of procedures in the file does not matter. `main` can call a procedure that is declared below it.
procedures.lesson.12: Parameters cannot be changed inside the procedure: `n = 5` is an error when `n` is a parameter. If you need a changeable copy, write `n := n` at the start of the procedure.
procedures.card.1: `add :: proc(a, b: int) -> int { return a + b }`
procedures-1.explain: The inner call gives `6`, the outer call doubles it again to `12`.
procedures-2.explain: `swap` returns the two values in the other order, so `x` is `2` and `y` is `1`.
procedures-3.prompt: Which line correctly starts a procedure that takes an `int` and returns an `int`?
procedures-3.explain: Name, `::`, `proc`, the parameters with `name: type` and the return type after `->`.
procedures-4.statement: A procedure in Odin can return more than one value.
procedures-4.explain: Write the types in parentheses, like `-> (int, int)`, and return the values separated by commas.
procedures-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 7.
procedures-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Hi, Ada.
procedures-6.explain: A parameter is written `name: type`, with a single colon.
procedures-7.prompt: Build the first line of a procedure `square` that takes an `int` `n` and returns an `int`.
procedures-7.explain: Name, `::`, `proc` with the parameters, then `->` and the return type.

procedures-8.explain: First 2 is squared to 4, then 1 is added. In the other order the result would be 9.

procedures-12.explain: `inc` gets a copy of `x` and returns `x + 1`. The variable `x` itself stays `5`.
arrays.title: Arrays and slices
arrays.summary: Store many values in fixed arrays, look at parts of them with slices, and grow lists with dynamic arrays.
arrays.lesson.0: A **fixed array** holds a fixed number of values of one type. `[3]int` is an array of three `int` values. You reach an element with its **index** in square brackets. The first index is `0`. `len(a)` gives the number of elements.
arrays.lesson.2: `for value in arr` goes through all elements. With `for value, i in arr` you also get the index. Note the order: the value comes first, then the index.
arrays.lesson.5: A **slice** is a view of a part of an array. Its type is written without a size, like `[]int`. `a[1:4]` starts at index `1` and stops before index `4`. `a[:2]` starts at the beginning, `a[3:]` goes to the end. A slice does not copy the values: when you change the slice, you change the array.
arrays.lesson.8: A **dynamic array**, like `[dynamic]int`, can grow. `append(&list, value)` adds values at the end. The `&` gives `append` the address of the variable, so it can change it. A dynamic array uses memory that you give back with `delete(list)`. `defer` runs a line at the end of the procedure, so you can write `defer delete(list)` right after you create the list.
arrays.lesson.10: A procedure that takes a slice works with every kind of array. Write `arr[:]` to pass a whole array or dynamic array as a slice.
arrays.lesson.12: An index must be smaller than the length. In `[3]int` the last index is `2`, and `a[3]` is an error. A fixed array cannot grow: only dynamic arrays work with `append`.
arrays.card.2: `a[1:3]` is a slice from index 1 to 2
arrays.card.4: `for v, i in a { }` value and index

arrays-4.explain: Indexes start at `0`. In `[3]string{"x", "y", "z"}` the element `"x"` has the index `0`.

structs.title: Structs and enums
structs.summary: Group values in structs, change them through pointers, and use enums with switch.
structs.lesson.0: A **struct** groups several values under one name. You declare it with `::` and `struct`. Each **field** has a name and a type, and a comma follows each field. You reach a field with a dot: `p.x`.
structs.lesson.2: You can name the fields when you create a struct: `Player{name = "Ada", level = 2}`. Fields that you leave out get their zero value.
structs.lesson.4: A procedure gets a copy of a struct. To change the original, pass a **pointer**: the type `^Player` means "pointer to a `Player`", and `&hero` gives the address of `hero`. Through the pointer, `p.level` reaches the field of the original.
structs.lesson.7: An **enum** is a type with a fixed list of named values. You write a value as `Direction.East`. When Odin already knows the type, `.West` is enough. `println` prints the name of the value.
structs.lesson.9: A `switch` over an enum has one case for each value. Odin checks that you did not forget a value: a missing case is an error.
structs.lesson.11: If you really want to handle only some values, write `#partial switch` instead of `switch`.
structs.lesson.12: Assigning a struct copies it: after `q := p`, changing `q.x` does not change `p.x`. Use a pointer when you want to change the original.
structs-1.explain: `r.w` is `3` and `r.h` is `4`, so the product is `12`.
structs-2.explain: `println` prints the name of an enum value.
structs-3.prompt: `Point` is a struct with the fields `x` and `y`. Which code creates a `Point` with `x` equal to 1 and `y` equal to 2?
structs-3.explain: A struct literal uses braces, and named fields use `=`.
structs-4.statement: Fields that you leave out in a struct literal get their zero value.
structs-4.explain: `Point{x = 5}` sets `x` to `5`, and `y` gets the zero value `0`.

structs-5.explain: `grow` changes the original, so it takes a pointer: `^Box`.

maps.title: Maps and strings
maps.summary: Look up values by key with maps, and work with text using len, slices and the strings package.
maps.lesson.0: A **map** stores values under **keys**. `map[string]int` has `string` keys and `int` values. You create a map with `make`, and you give its memory back with `delete`. `m[key] = value` adds or changes an entry, and `m[key]` reads it.
maps.lesson.2: A key that is not in the map gives the zero value. To find out if a key exists, write `value, ok := m[key]`: `ok` is `true` only when the key exists. `key in m` gives the same answer. `delete_key(&m, key)` removes an entry.
maps.lesson.4: `for key, value in m` goes through all entries. The order of the entries is not fixed, so do not rely on it. The name `_` throws away a value that you do not need.
maps.lesson.7: For a `string`, `len(s)` gives its length in bytes. For English letters, that is the number of characters. `s[1:3]` is a part of the string, like a slice of an array. `for c in s` goes through the characters one by one.
maps.lesson.9: The package `core:strings` has helpers for text. `strings.contains` and `strings.has_prefix` answer with a `bool`, and `strings.index` gives the position of a text, or `-1` if it is not there. `strings.to_upper` creates a new string, so give its memory back with `delete`.
maps.lesson.11: `strings.split` cuts a string into a slice of strings. `strings.join` puts strings together with a separator between them. Both create new memory.
maps.lesson.13: `+` joins only fixed texts like `"ab" + "cd"`. For variables, use `strings.concatenate({a, b})`.
maps-1.explain: The third assignment replaces the value of `"a"` with `7`, and `7 + 5` is `12`.
maps-2.explain: The word has 11 letters. `s[0:3]` contains the indexes 0, 1 and 2.
maps-3.explain: The key `"x"` does not exist, so you get the zero value `0` and `ok` is `false`.
maps-4.statement: A `for` loop over a map always visits the keys in the order in which you added them.
maps-4.explain: The order of the entries in a map is not fixed. If you need an order, keep the keys in an array.
